title: Heat Pump vs Oil, Propane and Baseboard Heat

narration.licence: draft only: unofficial Microsoft Edge read-aloud API, no terms for published media

sentences.text: If your house runs on propane, heating oil or electric baseboards, someone has probably told you a heat pump is the easy win.
But does a heat pump always beat each of them on running cost, or does one of them break the rule?

sentences.text: So who is right? Start with the widest view.

A national study estimated that among homes heating mainly with electricity, fuel oil or propane that already have air conditioning, 95 to 100 percent would see lower bills with a heat pump, depending on its efficiency.
The median saving it estimated was $300 to $650 a year.

sentences.text: An evaluation of ductless mini-split heat pumps found them more cost-effective than electric resistance and propane heat at every energy price and every outdoor temperature it examined.

excerpt.doc: Cadmus 2016, ductless mini-split evaluation (MA and RI)
excerpt.text:
The cost-effectiveness of DMSHPs used for heating depends on alternative heating systems, energy
prices for a given period, and outside air temperatures. Compared against electrical resistance and
propane heating, DMSHPs proved more cost-effective for all energy prices (using the same energy
source) and all outdoor air temperatures. For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the
temperature above which a DMSHP became more cost-effective. Given low current oil prices, relative to
historic values, DMSHPs offer cost-effective heating when compared to oil but only for temperature
ranges discussed in this report. A DMSHP, however, seldom proved cost-effective when compared to
natural gas heating systems (excepting a scenario where a DMSHP heats single space, thus negating the
need to turn on a whole house heating system).
excerpt.highlight: DMSHPs proved more cost-effective for all energy prices

sentences.text: If you heat with propane or baseboards, get installed quotes and set them against what you spend on fuel each winter.
If you heat with oil, ask a different question: at this winter's oil and electricity prices, below what outdoor temperature does your old system run cheaper, and will you keep it for those days?
